Vaiṣṇavism
------------------------------------------
General Introduction
Whether विष्णु is one of the Hindu Trinity entrusted with the task of sustenance of the world or an aspect of आदित्य (the Sun-god) or the all-pervading cosmic deity (from the root-verb viṣḷ = to pervade) there is no doubt that he is one of the most popular and widely worshipped gods of the Hindus.
Though he is often associated closely with इन्द्र in the Ṛgveda he never loses his prominence. His immense power to occupy and transcend the three worlds as Urukrama (Vāmana), his supreme unconquerable strength, his limitless compassion towards his devotees, his being the protector of all and his supremely sweet abode (the paramapada) have been described in several mantras (vide Ṛgveda 1.155.5; 6.69.8; 7.25.12; 3.55.10; 1.154.5). The best way to please him is through sacrificial offerings (ibid 7.40.5) and hymns of praise (ibid 1.156.3).
However, by the time of the epics and the पुराणस्, he grows in stature occupying the highest position among the gods of the Hindu pantheon.
‘Nārāyaṇa’ is another name by which he is known even in the Vedic literature as also in the epics and the पुराणस्.
Being the deity responsible for the sthiti or protection of the created world, he is often obliged to come down as an अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन्. Though the number of such avatāras can be limitless—and sometimes as many as 23 are mentioned—somehow the ten known as the Daśāva-tāras, have attained a traditional sanction and a religious status.
Gradually, over the centuries, a philo-sophy and a religion centred round विष्णु evolved into a regular system now called वैष्णविस्म्. Bhāgavatamata is another name by which this system has been known.
(See धर्म">BHĀGAVATADHARMA for details.)
The Nārāyaṇīya section of the epic Mahābhārata (vide शान्तिपर्व, Chapters 334-351) seems to be the earliest systematisation of वैष्णविस्म्. Other sources are: Bhagavadgītā, Viṣṇupurāṇa, Bhāgavata, Pāñcarātra and Vaikhānasa Āgamas and Bhaktisūtras of नारद and शाण्डिल्य.
Attention has to be drawn to another development in the evolution of Vaiṣṇa-vism. Though कृष्ण was listed as the ninth अवतार in the list of दशावतारस्, he was gradually elevated and made identical with विष्णु-नारायण, the ten avatāras being considered his avatāras. Thus the कृष्ण cult got merged with the Bhāgavatamata. Since कृष्ण or कृष्ण-वासुदेव, belonged to the सात्वत clan of the यदु race, Sātvatamata is another name by which it came to be known.
Various Schools of Vaiṣṇavism
The basic structure of वैष्णविस्म् as revealed in some of the earliest sources like the Nārāyaṇīya advocated the supremacy of विष्णु-नारायण as God and भक्ति or devotion to him as the chief means of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्. However, different ways of expounding it by the various ācāryas (religious teachers) gave rise, in course of time, to different sects and subsects of वैष्णविस्म्. The more prominent ones among them may now be described briefly.
The Āḷvārs
They were the earliest Vaiṣṇava teachers known to history. They belonged to Tamil Nadu and lived probably during the period 2nd to the 8th century A. D. Among them were saints from all castes and included a woman (Godādevī) also.
They taught that विष्णु-नारायण was the Supreme God and भक्ति or devotion to him was the means of लिबेरतिओन्. They accepted the avatāras (incarnations) of विष्णु such as राम and कृष्ण and advocated the importance of अर्चा or ritualistic worship with the strong faith that God descends into the icon in a subtle form during the worship.
Rāmānuja (A.

-1137)
To Rāmānuja, the ब्रह्मन् or ईश्वर of Vedānta is actually नारायण (or विष्णु) inseparably associated with Śrī or लक्ष्मी. नारायण creates the world with his twofold प्रकृति (basic nature), the अचित् (insentient matter) and the cit (sentient beings, the jīvas or individual souls). He sustains it and, at the end of a cycle, withdraws it.
Śrī or लक्ष्मी is his divine consort, the personification of his compassion. She intervenes with नारायण on behalf of the jīvas and gets them what they want, including लिबेरतिओन्.
Bhakti or devotion to both of them is the chief means of लिबेरतिओन्.
Since Rāmānuja gives equal importance to Śrī (or लक्ष्मी) along with विष्णु-नारायण, his system is known as श्रीवैष्णविस्म्.
See also RĀMĀNUJĀCĀRYA, ŚRĪVAIṢṆA-VISM and VIŚIṢṬĀDVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.
Madhva (A.

-1317)
The credit for establishing Vaiṣṇa-vism on a firm foundation and making it popular among the masses should go to Madhva or मध्वाचार्य. His philosophy, known as द्वैत Vedānta, can be summed up as follows: ‘Śrīhari (Viṣṇu-नारायण) is the highest truth who can be known only through the वेदस्. The created world is real. The jīvas are all different from one another and are dependent on Śrīhari. Among them also, there are differences of quality and status. मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् is actually the experiencing of one’s real nature as आनन्द or bliss. This can be got through pure devotion to Śrīhari.’
From this philosophy of devotion to विष्णु evolved the various corollaries such as ritualistic worship and devotional singing, giving rise to a regular movement of saints of devotion.
See DĀSAKŪṬA and DVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.
Nimbārka (12th century A. D.)
Nimbārka’s philosophy is known as द्वैताद्वैत.
Parabrahman or God is कृष्ण. He is the supreme independent reality. The jīvātmas (individual souls) are infinite in number and are atomic in size. प्रकृति is insentient nature out of which the world is made. The jīvas and प्रकृति are dependent realities ever inseparable from परब्रह्मन्. The relationship between them is like that of the sea and the waves or the sun and its rays.
Bhakti or devotion to Kṛṣna along with राधा, surrender to them and obedience to the गुरु or spiritual teacher are the chief means of लिबेरतिओन्.
Nimbārka was the first Vaiṣṇava teacher to introduce राधा as कृष्ण-शक्ति or divine consort.
Rāmānanda (A.

-1470)
Though ordained by a monk of the Rāmānuja sect of वैष्णविस्म्, रामानन्द deviated from it in advocating devotion to राम as the best means of लिबेरतिओन् and initiated persons of all castes into his cult. कबीर् (A.
-1518), barber Senā (of Maharashtra) and पद्मावती, a woman, were among his group of disciples. Tulasīdās (A.

-1623) was a follower of रामानन्द’s path of devotion.
He succeeded to a great extent in spreading वैष्णविस्म् with राम as the central deity.
Kabīrdās (A.

-1518)
Prominent among the leaders of the भक्ति movement of the Middle-Ages, कबीर् (supposed to be a Muslim) was a disciple of रामानन्द. Devotion to राम, ignoring the many social conventions, was the path he accepted and preached. In course of time his followers formed a separate sect in his name and came to be known as Kabīrpanthis.
Vallabha (A.

-1531)
Originally hailing from the Telugu country (the present Andhra Pradesh) वल्लभ settled down in वृन्दाबन्. He was not only a great scholar but also a great devotee. He further strengthened the movement of Kṛṣṇabhakti.
Himself remaining a householder he preached an easy path of worship of and total surrender to कृष्ण. Like रामानन्द he too accepted disciples from all castes and even from other religions. His disciples were responsible for building temples of कृष्ण and spreading the sect.
Puṣṭimārga (‘path of spiritual nourishment’) which advocates the path of total self-surrender to God receiving proper initiation from a qualified गुरु is वल्लभ’s special contribution.
See also PUṢṬIMĀRGA.
Caitanya (A.

-1533)
Caitanya or Śrīkṛṣna चैतन्य, who hailed from Bengal, is another bright jewel shining brilliantly among the leaders of वैष्णविस्म्.
Though an unrivalled scholar, especially in लोगिच्, revelling in defeating other scholars, he was totally transformed into an equally unrivalled devotee of कृष्ण, by Īśvarapurī, a saṁnyāsin of the Mādhva Order.
Group-singing of devotional songs on कृष्ण and dancing in his name—generally called Saṅkīrtan—are his contribution.
He propagated a philosophy known as Acintyabhedābheda and tried to wipe off caste distinctions in the name of कृष्ण.
His followers consider him a combined इन्चर्नतिओन् of राधा and कृष्ण.
See also ACINTYA-BHEDĀBHEDA SCHOOL.
Spread of Vaiṣṇavism
Vaiṣṇavism, as an important aspect of the भक्ति Movement, spread all over the land—the Indian peninsula—right from the 13th century up to the 18th. Broadly speaking, there were two important streams centred round राम and कृष्ण, the latter being much more popular.
The राम sect which was ushered in by रामानन्द and कबीर्, was sustained and developed by Gosvāmi तुलसी-dās (A.

-1847) as also their disciples.
As regards the Kṛṇa sects they are legion.
The saints of Maharashtra, led by Sant Jñāneśvar (end of the 13th century A. D.) and followed by other saintly devotees such as नाम्देव् (A.

-1694) revolutionised the way of life of the common folk with the पाण्डुरङ्ग-Viṭṭhala cult. Closely akin to it and on almost parallel lines was the Kṛṣṇabhakti movement of the Haridāsas of Karnataka like पुरन्दरदास (A.

-1564), कनकदास (15th century A. D.) and विजयदास (1687-1755).
In the Hindi belt of North India it was left to the blind saint सूर्दास् (A.

-1547) to popularise devotion to कृष्ण.
Mention should also be made of Narasī Mehtā (A.

-1569) of Assam who spread the कृष्ण cult in their regions.
The भक्ति Movement of these musician-saints made religion simple and practical for the common people. It also successfully reclaimed many of them who had gone outside the Hindu fold.
Conclusion
Vaiṣṇavism like शैविस्म्, is an important aspect of हिन्दुइस्म्. Though rooted in the Vedic concept of dedication to विष्णु, it has, over the centuries, expanded enormously both in depth and width, fulfilling a great psychological need of the Hindu society. That is why it is a formidable force to reckon with even to this day as reflected in the spate of Vaiṣṇava temples and festivals.

Vaiśampāyana
------------------------------------------
He was one of the four chief disciples of व्यास to whom the Yajurveda had been taught. The sage Yājñnavalkya was his nephew and disciple who later left him.
He taught the Mahābhārata to जनमेजय (vide Ādiparva

Vaiśvadeva
(‘pertaining to all the gods’)
------------------------------------------
This is the first of the four वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् listed under चातुर्मास्य (See CĀTURMĀSYA.). It is performed mainly to attain हेअवेन् and is spread over two days.
On the first day an oblation with the pañcahotṛ formula (a mystical मन्त्र in which five priests are mentioned) and a cake are offered to the वैश्वानर अग्नि (fire-god).
A new fire is generated on the second day mixed with the existing आहवनीय fire. This is followed by several steps of the sacrifice which are too complicated to mention.
The left-over offering of Vājina (liquid portion of ‘broken’ milk) has to be consumed by the sacrificer.

Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata
------------------------------------------
Purāṇas are the most popular literature of the Hindus, especially among the masses. Out of the 18 major पुराणस्, Bhāgavata is an important work. But, there are two Bhāgavatas extant, one dealing with the supremacy of the देवी, Śaktī or the Divine मोथेर्, and the other, with that of विष्णु. The former is called Devī-bhāgavata and the latter simply as Bhāgavata. However, to distinguish the latter from the former, an appellation ‘Vaiṣṇava’ is sometimes added, making it the Vaiṣṇava Bhāgavata.
It is the latter that is generally classed among the 18 major पुराणस्.
See also BHĀGAVATA and DEVĪ-BHĀGAVATA.

Vaiṣṇavī
------------------------------------------
Listed among the सप्तमातृकास् (the Seven Mothers), वैष्णवी is the शक्ति (power-goddess) of Lord विष्णु.
In the Durgāsaptaśatī (8.18) she is described as an emanation—one of the seven—of दुर्गा.
She is identical in form with विष्णु. She is dark in complexion and wears yellow silken robes as also a वनमाला (garland of wild flowers). She has four hands holding चक्र (discus), शङ्ख (conch), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). Sometimes she is shown with six hands, the last two showing the gestures of abhaya (protection from fear) and varada (giving boons).
She rides on the गरुड, the famous vulture-mount of विष्णु.

Vaiśeṣika Darśana
------------------------------------------
Introduction
The वैशेषिक दर्शन was founded by कणाद, also known as Ulūka. Hence it is also called Kāṇāda or Aulūkya दर्शन. कणाद seems to be a nickname of Ulūka since he led the life of an ascetic. He used to live on kaṇas or grains gleaned from agricultural fields (kaṇa = grain; ad = to eat).
The basic text is the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras of कणाद. It is divided into ten adhyāyas or chapters, each adhyāya containing two āhnikas or sections. It has 374 sūtras in all.
The earliest exposition of this work seems to be the Padārtha-धर्म-saṅgraha of प्रशस्तपाद (5th century A. D.). Though known as Bhāṣya, it is not a regular sūtra-by-sūtra commentary on the original work. This Bhāṣya, while restating the principles contained in the original sūtras, develops them considerably. The Nyāyakandalī of Śrīdhara (991 A. D.), Vyomavatī of Vyomaśiva and Kiraṇā-valī of उदयन (A.

) are the well-known commentaries of प्रशस्तपाद. Vallabhācārya’s (11th cent. A. D.) Nyāya-līlāvatī and उदयन’s Lakṣaṇāvalī are two valuable compendiums on this system.
The Vaiśeṣika system became closely associated with the न्याय system in course of time, so much so, that the later writers started dealing with them as if they were one system. Of these, mention must be made of the Saptapadārthī of Śivāditya (10th cent. A. D.) and the Bhāṣā-pariccheda of Viśvanātha (A.

).
The saptapadārthas or seven categories are:
dravya (substance);
guṇa (quality);
karma (action);
sāmānya (generality);
viśeṣa (particularity);
samavāya (relation of inherence), and
abhāva (non-existence).
These may now be considered one by one.
DRAVYA is a substance in which a गुण (quality) and कर्म (action) can exist. It is the substratum for both.
There are nine kinds of dravyas: the four elements (earth, water, light and air, respectively called पृथ्वी, jala, तेजस् and वायु); आकाश (ether); kāla (time); dik (space); आत्मन् (soul) and मनस् (mind). All these are eternal.
The four elements exist in the form of paramāṇus (atoms) before च्रेअतिओन्.
Ākāśa, kāla, dik and आत्मन् are all-pervading whereas मनस् is aṇu (atomic) in size.
The Vaiśeṣika system accepts two kinds of souls: the jīvātmans and परमात्मन् (also known as ईश्वर or महेश्वर). The former ones are infinite in number whereas परमात्मन्, the Supreme सोउल् or God, is only one.
GUṆA or quality is always dependent on द्रव्य or substance for its existence and manifestation. It belongs to a द्रव्य but never to another गुण.
The Vaiśeṣika system enumerates the guṇas as 24. Some of them are: the five qualities of the five sense-organs, pari-māṇa (magnitude), saṁyoga (conjunction), बुद्धि (cognition), sukha and दुःख (pleasure and pain), icchā and द्वेष (desire and aversion), saṁskāra (tendency), धर्म and अधर्म (merit and demerit).
This enumeration limiting the guṇas to 24, has been done from the standpoint of their impossibility of further division.
KARMA or action is physical movement. It belongs to a substance and is dynamic in nature. Five kinds of action like utkṣepaṇa (throwing upward) and ākuñcana (contraction) have been listed. They can be perceived by the senses of sight and touch.
Manas or मिन्द् too has movement but it is not perceived externally.
SĀMĀNYA or generality is the essence in a class and can be called the universal. These universals are नित्य (eternal) and inhere in the individuals. For example, gotva (cowness) and ghaṭatva (jarness) are present in each individual cow and jar respectively. The death of a cow or the breaking of a jar do not destroy the सामान्य that was in them.
VIŚEṢA or particularity is the direct opposite of the सामान्य. It is the unique individuality of the eternal substances. For instance, one परमाणु or atom of earth is distinct from another परमाणु, also of earth. There is something in these atoms which makes them different from one another. That is viśeṣa.
SAMAVĀYA or inherence seems to be a special concept contributed by the Vaiśeṣika philosophy. Saṁyoga or conjunction between two objects can be brought about at will; so also viyoga or disjunction. This relationship between two objects is temporary. But the समवाय relationship is inherent in the substances. (Hence they are called ‘ayutasiddha’ or related without conjunction.) It is नित्य or permanent. The relation by which a whole is in its parts (e.g., the cloth in its threads), a quality like redness in a red object like a red rose, a movement in a moving object (e.g., a moving ball), is समवाय or inherence. The terms related by समवाय are not reversible.
ABHĀVA or non-existence (the last) is the only category of the negative type. It is considered as a reality in this system. When we look at the sky in the night, we recognise the non-existence of the sun there, even as we notice the existence of the मोओन् and the स्तर्स्. Broadly speaking, अभाव is of two types: saṁsargābhāva and अन्योन्याभाव. The former is the absence of something in something else, as the non-existence of a jar on a table. In the latter case, it simply means that one thing is not another thing, as a horse not being present in a buffalo.
Saṁsargābhāva is of three kinds:
prāgabhāva (antecedent non-existence);
pradhvaṁsābhāva or dhvaṁsā-भाव (non-existence after destruction); and,
atyantābhāva (absolute non-existence).
Non-existence of the होउसे in the bricks, before it is built, is the example for प्रागभाव. Non-existence of an earthen jar in the broken pieces, after the jar is broken, is the example for pradhvaṁsā-भाव. Absence of colour or shape in air is the example for अत्यन्ताभाव.
God and the World
The वैशेषिक दर्शन accepts the existence of God—called ईश्वर or Maheśvara—as the Supreme Intelligent Being under whose will and guidance this world is created, sustained and destroyed.
This world is a system of physical things and the living beings which interact with one another. What guides the world is actually the moral order, by which the life and destiny of all the individual souls are governed, the universal law of कर्म.
The starting point of च्रेअतिओन् (followed by sustenance and destruction, these three being cyclic and eternal) is the will of God. The first product of his will to create, is the World-सोउल्, ब्रह्मा. He is infilled by God with the six blessed qualities like ज्ञान, वैराग्य and ऐश्वर्य (knowledge, detachment and splendour). It is this ब्रह्मा the chief architect of च्रेअतिओन्, who proceeds with further च्रेअतिओन् in accordance with the totality of the adṛṣṭas (the unseen merits and demerits) of the individual souls by setting in motion the paramāṇus or atoms to combine with one another, ultimately resulting in the world.
The process of dissolution is in the reverse order. ब्रह्मा gives up his body. महेश्वर then wills the dissolution and brings about the प्रलय or destruction. The whole world is then reduced to its primary state of the seven padārthas.
Conclusion
Like the न्याय system, the वैशेषिक दर्शन also is a realistic philosophy which combines pluralism with theism. च्रेअतिओन् is not by chance but executed by God in a planned manner, as per the karmas of the individual souls, for the proper realisation of their ultimate moral perfection.
By harmonising the atomic theory with a moral and spiritual outlook on life and accepting God as the creator and moral governor of the world, the Vaiśeṣika system moved nearer towards the Vedānta system which proved to be the pinnacle of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् as a whole.

Vaishno Devi
------------------------------------------
The वैस्ह्नो देवि is an important cave temple nestled in the Himālayan ranges of the Jammu region of the Jammu and Kashmir State. It is dedicated to the goddess दुर्गा in her three aspects of Mahāsarasvatī, महालक्ष्मी and Mahākālī as described in the well-known work, the Durgāsaptaśatī or the Caṇḍī. The sanctum contains three separate bulbous forms in stone, called Piṇḍīs, all rising from the same base stone. The first representing Mahāsarasvatī has a whitish tinge. The second called महालक्ष्मी is yellowish red in colour. The last, that of Mahākālī, is black.
वैस्ह्नो देवि">Shrine at Vaishno DeviThe whole shrine is in a natural rock form.
The origins of this cave shrine are unknown.
According to the local legends a pious ब्राह्मण, Paṇḍit Śrīdhar by name, lived at the foot of Trikūṭa (the mountain where the shrine is situated) about 700 years back. Due to his intense devotion and earnest prayers, the Divine मोथेर् had manifested herself as a little girl of extraordinary beauty and had fed a very large crowd of people invited by Śrīdhar. This place is now called Bhūmikā Mandir. She had also spent nine months in meditation in a cave, now known as the Garbh Joon. When pursued by the demon Bhairon (Bhairava?), she beheaded him, assuming the fierce form of Caṇḍikā. At the request of the dying demon, she granted the boon that her devotees should also visit the place of his death, where a temple stands now, called Bhairon Mandir.
The other holy places associated with this legend are the Bāṇ गङ्गा river (also called Bāl गङ्गा) produced by the arrow shot by the मोथेर् and the Caraṇapādukā temple containing her footprints on a rock.
Pilgrims travel up to the small town of Katra which is 48 kms. (30 miles) from Jammu. The ascent to the cave starts from here, the distance being 12 kms. (7.5 miles). On the way are situated the Bāṇ गङ्गा temple, the Caraṇapādukā temple and the halfway point called Ardh Kuvari near which is the cave Garbh Joon.
The वैस्ह्नो देवि temple is situated at a height of 1700 metres (5200 ft.) above the sea-level. It is a cave 30 metres (93 ft.) long and 1.5 metres (5 ft.) high.
A lamp is kept burning always. The shrine is kept open round the clock.
Pilgrims have to wade through ankle or knee-deep icy water in the cave to have a view of the deity. The movement is by bending and crawling since the height inside the cave does not permit standing.
After this, the devotees are expected to visit the Bhairon Temple situated at a distance of 2.5 kms. (1½ miles) from the main shrine and at a height of 2010 metres (6700 ft.).
Ceremonial worship is done to the goddess twice a day, at sunrise and sunset. Each time it lasts for about two hours. During these periods, pilgrims are not allowed inside.
The main celebrations and festivals are during the नवरात्र period (in September/October) when a Śatacaṇḍīyāga is organised.
Since A.

, the shrine complex is being ably managed by the ‘Shri Mata वैस्ह्नो देवि Shrine Board’.
Facilities provided for the pilgrims include steps, tracks, resthouses, living rooms, messes providing good ड़ोओद्, medical attention, stores and cloakrooms.

Vaiśvānara
(‘one who leads all human beings’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in several senses. It is one of the names of अग्नि, fire or fire-god.
The Bhagavadgītā (15.14) refers to it as an aspect of कृष्ण (or God) who resides in the bodies of living beings and digests the ड़ोओद् they eat (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9.1 also).
In the Vedānta philosophy it refers to ब्रह्मन् / आत्मन् as चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, associated with the whole created world (vide Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 3). The Vedāntasāra of सदानन्द calls him as Virāṭ also (para 111).
He is called वैश्वानर since he leads all human beings according their पुण्य (merit) or पाप (demerit) to the respective goals.
